rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: A biological agent is a micro-organism or other agent that can cause infection, allergy, toxicity or another hazard to human health.

rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: COSHH is the main legislation for controlling workplace exposure to biological agents and requires risk assessment and prevention or adequate control.

rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: Incidental exposure can arise from blood or body fluids, contaminated water, waste, laundry, animals or similar materials encountered during work.

rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: Risk assessments must identify workers and other people who could be exposed, including vulnerable workers, contractors, visitors and members of the public.

rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: Employers should first consider removing the biological hazard and then use suitable engineering, organisational and hygiene controls.

rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: Biological agents used deliberately are classified into four hazard groups according to disease severity, spread risk and availability of treatment or prophylaxis.

rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: Deliberate work can require containment measures, records of exposed workers and notification or licensing before specified activities.

rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: People working with biological agents should review the current Approved List and apply controls appropriate to the agent's hazard-group classification.

rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: Biological-agent controls depend on agent classification, transmission route, concentration, activity, containment, worker susceptibility, environmental survival and emergency arrangements.

rows.source: HSE biological agents and infection control
rows.verified: Biological-agent evidence is agent-, activity-, workplace- and person-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: Blood-contaminated sharps can transmit hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: Employers must manage sharps risks where workers use sharps, handle them after use or may encounter discarded sharps during their work.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: The sharps risk assessment should identify hazards, consider the nature of the work and implement, monitor and review controls.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: Where possible, dutyholders should consider safer sharp devices and methods that keep hands away from the sharp.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: Needles should not be bent or forced, and sharps should be handled so their points are directed away from hands and the body.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: Workers need training in safe use, disposal and the response required after a sharps injury.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: Used sharps should be disposed of immediately in an appropriate sharps container and should not normally be reused, resheathed or recapped.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: Healthcare employers must have arrangements covering safe sharps use and disposal, training and procedures for responding to injuries.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: Sharps controls depend on device, procedure, patient or material contamination, user competence, disposal route, staffing, environment and post-exposure response.

rows.source: HSE needlestick and sharps safety
rows.verified: Sharps evidence is device-, task-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection or injury probability.
